title: Choosing Between ELN and LIMS: Which Does Your Lab Need?
summary: Choosing between ELN and LIMS? Compare workflows, sample tracking, experiment documentation, and integration needs to decide which system your lab should implement first.
body_markdown:
## TL;DR


- Choose an **ELN** when your biggest need is documenting experiments, protocols, observations, and scientific decisions.
- Choose a **LIMS** when your biggest need is tracking samples, standardizing tests, managing results, and controlling repeatable workflows.
- Consider both when your lab needs flexible research documentation alongside structured sample and testing operations.
- Before buying, map your workflows, existing tools, integration needs, and the records each system must manage.


Choosing between an **electronic lab notebook (ELN) and a laboratory information management system (LIMS)** is not just a software comparison. It is a decision about how your lab documents scientific work, tracks samples, manages results, and connects data across workflows.


ELN, LIMS, or both? Start by identifying the right setup for your lab.


[Explore Scispot](https://www.scispot.com/demo-request)


The right starting point depends on the work your team performs every day. A research group running exploratory experiments may prioritize an ELN, while a quality control laboratory processing recurring tests may need a LIMS first. Some organizations need both, but they do not always need to purchase or implement both at the same time.


Here is how to decide which system fits your lab.


## Understand What Each System Is Designed to Do


### What does an ELN do?


An electronic lab notebook provides a structured digital environment for documenting scientific experiments. Scientists use it to record protocols, observations, calculations, images, results, and conclusions.


An ELN is particularly useful when experiments change frequently and the reasoning behind a result matters as much as the result itself.


Consider an early-stage biotech team evaluating several experimental conditions. Researchers need to record what they changed, why they changed it, what happened, and what they plan to test next. An ELN helps keep that context organized and searchable.


Keep experimental methods, observations, and scientific conclusions organized in one digital workspace.


[Explore Scispot ELN](https://www.scispot.com/elns)


### What does a LIMS do?


A laboratory information management system focuses on structured laboratory operations. It commonly manages sample registration, identifiers, sample locations, test assignments, workflow status, results, and reporting.


A LIMS becomes especially valuable when samples move through defined steps and the lab needs consistent tracking across analysts, instruments, tests, or locations.


For example, a diagnostics or pharmaceutical QC laboratory may need to register incoming samples, assign tests, capture results, route records for review, and maintain traceability throughout the process.


Bring structure to sample intake, test assignments, and result tracking as your lab grows.


[Explore Scispot LIMS](https://www.scispot.com/lims)


### ELN vs LIMS: The practical difference


Decision factor ELN LIMS


Primary focus Experiments and scientific context Samples and laboratory operations


Typical record Experiment, protocol, observation Sample, test, result, status


Workflow style Flexible and exploratory Structured and repeatable


Main user need Understand and reproduce scientific work Track and manage laboratory work at scale


Common starting point Research and development QC, testing, diagnostics, sample-heavy operations


These are general patterns, not rigid rules. Modern platforms can combine both capabilities. Evaluate the depth of the functions your team actually needs, not just the software category.


## When Should You Choose an ELN First?


An ELN is often the better starting point when your main operational problem is how scientific knowledge is captured, shared, and reused.


### Your experiments change frequently


If protocols evolve as researchers test hypotheses, a flexible notebook can be more useful than a system designed primarily around fixed sample-processing steps.


### Your team struggles to find experimental context


If scientists rely on paper notebooks, disconnected documents, spreadsheets, or scattered files, an ELN can help bring protocols, observations, attachments, and conclusions into searchable records.


### Reproducibility and collaboration are priorities


When several researchers need to understand or repeat an experiment, consistent documentation helps preserve the context behind the work.


**An ELN is a strong first choice when the central question is:** “What did we do, why did we do it, and what did we learn?”


Before implementing one, check whether it supports your experimental templates, data types, review processes, access controls, and integration requirements. If sample tracking is also a major operational challenge, include those needs in the evaluation.


## When Should You Choose a LIMS First?


A LIMS is often the better starting point when the lab's biggest challenge is controlling structured workflows and keeping track of samples and results.


### Sample tracking is becoming difficult


If staff spend time locating samples, reconciling identifiers, updating spreadsheets, or checking where work stands, a LIMS can provide a more consistent operational record.


### Your lab runs repeatable tests


Routine QC, contract testing, and diagnostics workflows often require samples to move through defined stages, with assigned tests, recorded results, review steps, and clear status visibility.


### You need more consistent result management


If your team manually transfers instrument outputs, struggles to consolidate results, or assembles reports from multiple sources, evaluate LIMS capabilities for instrument connectivity, structured data capture, and reporting.


**A LIMS is a strong first choice when the central question is:** “Where is this sample, what work has been performed, and what is its current result or status?”


Check that the system supports your sample types, workflow complexity, reporting requirements, integrations, and applicable quality controls. A LIMS should fit the actual process, not force the lab into an unsuitable workflow.


## When Does Your Lab Need Both an ELN and a LIMS?


Some laboratories need flexible experiment documentation and structured sample management. In those cases, an ELN and a LIMS can serve complementary purposes.


### Example: A biotech team moving from research to testing


Imagine a biotech team developing an assay and then transferring it into a repeatable testing process.


1. **During development:** Scientists use an ELN to document protocols, experimental conditions, observations, and method changes.
2. **During sample processing:** A LIMS tracks registered samples, assigned tests, workflow stages, and results.
3. **During review:** Scientists and lab operations staff connect the experimental context with the relevant sample and test records.
4. **As the process scales:** The team can standardize recurring workflows while preserving the scientific documentation needed to understand how the method developed.


The important point is not that every lab needs two products. It is that experiment documentation and sample operations may have different requirements, even when they belong to the same scientific process.


### Decide whether to integrate separate systems or use a connected platform


If your organization already has an ELN or LIMS that works well, replacing it may not be necessary. Assess whether the missing capability can be addressed through configuration, integration, or an additional system.


If you are starting from scratch, compare separate products with platforms that offer both ELN and LIMS capabilities in a connected environment.


In either case, ask how sample identifiers, experiment records, results, permissions, audit trails, and updates are linked. Confirm which system owns each record and how changes are handled.

## How to Make the Final Decision


Before selecting software, answer these five questions.


### 1. What is the biggest problem you need to solve?


Prioritize the operational issue that causes the most rework, delays, traceability gaps, or difficulty retrieving information. Avoid selecting software solely because it offers the longest feature list.


### 2. What does your workflow look like today?


Map the process from the first activity to the final record. Identify where experiments are documented, samples are registered, results are captured, and approvals occur.


### 3. Which systems do you already use?


Review existing notebooks, spreadsheets, instruments, databases, and business applications. Determine whether you need a new system, better integration, or more structured use of an existing platform.


### 4. What are your data integrity and compliance requirements?


For regulated workflows, assess relevant audit trails, electronic signatures, access controls, record retention, review procedures, and validation responsibilities. A software purchase alone does not establish compliance; the system must be appropriately configured, implemented, and governed.


### 5. What will implementation and future growth require?


Compare licensing, configuration, migration, integration, training, support, maintenance, and validation costs where applicable. Ask vendors to demonstrate representative workflows and explain how the system will adapt as your lab adds assays, sample types, instruments, users, or locations.


Compare your must-have workflows against a platform that brings ELN and LIMS capabilities together.

## Build a Lab Software Setup That Fits Your Work


The choice between an ELN and a LIMS comes down to your lab's primary workflow.


Choose an ELN first when flexible experiment documentation and scientific context are the biggest priorities. Choose a LIMS first when sample tracking, repeatable testing, and results management are the main challenges. Consider both when your lab needs the two capabilities to work together.


You do not necessarily need to replace your entire technology stack to improve laboratory operations. Start with the workflow creating the most friction, then determine which capabilities and connections will make the biggest difference.
